quote: Wenn auch noch alle Differentialquotien- ten nach der Fläche d. h. die Tangentialebenen etc. übereinstimmen, so werden dies die nothw. u. hin- reichenden Bedingungen sein, damit die Form $F \equiv 0$ nach dem vorgel. Modulsystem ist.
english: If in addition all differential quotients with respect to the surface, i.e. the tangent planes etc., agree, then these will be the necessary and sufficient conditions for the form F to be ≡ 0 with respect to the given module system.
topic: A dismissive remark on Christoffel's essay on irrational numbers, followed by a research programme on Noether's general theorem about surfaces through given points and curves, membership of a form in a module system, and a link to ideal theory.

triage.modern_statement: Let I ⊂ k[x_0,...,x_n] be a homogeneous ideal (Hilbert's 'Modulsystem') whose zero set is a given configuration of points and curves (or other subvarieties) on which a form F is supposed to vanish, as in Max Noether's AF+BG Fundamentalsatz and its generalisation to surfaces. Hilbert's conjecture: F ∈ I (that is, F ≡ 0 mod I) exactly when F vanishes on the zero set and, in addition, its derivatives 'along the surface' (tangent planes and higher-order contact) satisfy matching conditions. In modern terms this asks whether ideal membership can be decided by local conditions: vanishing on V(I) together with finitely many differential conditions at the components of I. The modern answer is primary decomposition plus Noetherian operators. F ∈ I if and only if, for each primary component Q with prime P, every one of a finite set of differential operators D_i (with polynomial coefficients) sends F into P, i.e. D_i F vanishes on V(P).
triage.answered_by: This was settled step by step rather than by one paper. Lasker (1905) and Emmy Noether (1921) gave primary decomposition, which reduces the question to local, component-by-component conditions. Macaulay's inverse systems (1916) and Gröbner's work (1930s–50s) recast the conditions as differential ones. Ehrenpreis and Palamodov (1960s, the Fundamental Principle) gave the first complete description of primary ideals by differential operators ('Noetherian operators'). Cid-Ruiz and Sturmfels (arXiv 2101.03643, 2021) produced 'differential primary decompositions', in which ideal membership is characterised by differential conditions and the minimal number of conditions equals the arithmetic multiplicity. Hilbert's own 1890/1893 work, including the Nullstellensatz, handled the radical (reduced) case. I found no source that names this diary note specifically. The attribution is my own match of the mathematical content.

evidence.claim: Ideal membership in a commutative ring can be characterised by differential conditions. The minimal number of conditions needed is the arithmetic multiplicity. This generalises the Noetherian operators of Ehrenpreis–Palamodov.

Gröbner was the first to address characterising ideal membership by differential conditions. The first complete description of primary ideals by differential operators came from analysts, in the Fundamental Principle of Ehrenpreis and Palamodov.

A primary ideal in a polynomial ring is described by its variety plus a finite set of Noetherian operators (differential operators with polynomial coefficients). Symbolic and numerical algorithms for computing them now exist.
Max Noether's 1873 Fundamental ('AF+BG') Theorem, the starting point of Hilbert's programme, combines geometric (local) conditions with membership of a form in an ideal.
Fulton's modern account of Noether's Fundamentalsatz, via adjoints and conductors, for curves on nonsingular surfaces.

triage.why: The note proposes a local criterion for when a form lies in a 'Modulsystem' (an ideal): vanishing at the given points and curves plus agreement of derivatives (tangent planes etc.), as a higher-dimensional Noether AF+BG theorem. Taken literally, first-order tangency conditions are not enough for non-reduced components; higher-order and more subtle differential conditions are needed. The correct general form is the Lasker–Noether primary decomposition combined with Macaulay/Gröbner inverse systems and Ehrenpreis–Palamodov Noetherian operators, which make 'necessary and sufficient differential conditions' exact. The topic is active today: there is a 2021 theory of differential primary decomposition and Macaulay2 software for Noetherian operators. Confidence is medium because the note is informal and I found no source that discusses this specific diary entry. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem.
